## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature and SuttaCentral)
*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and SuttaCentral data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*
The *Caṅkī Sutta* (MN 95; PTS MN ii 164) is an important discourse of the *Majjhimanikāya* addressing the epistemological status of Vedic revelation and the nature of spiritual education [SuttaCentral; Kalupahana 1976; Jayatilleke 1963]. Set in Kosala, the narrative opens with the renowned brahmin Caṅkī going to visit the Buddha despite objections from his fellow brahmins [SuttaCentral; Traces of Gandhāran Buddhism]. In the ensuing discussion, a precocious young brahmin student named Kāpaṭhika intervenes to affirm the undisputed validity of the ancient Vedic hymns [SuttaCentral; Jayatilleke 1963]. The Buddha criticizes reliance on unbroken oral tradition (*anussava*), comparing the succession of Vedic teachers to a line of blind men clinging to one another (*paramparāsaṁsattā*), wherein neither the first, middle, nor last can see [Jayatilleke 1963; Seeger 2005].
Central to the sutta is the Buddha's epistemological distinction among five grounds for accepting a view—faith (*saddhā*), personal preference (*ruci*), tradition (*anussava*), rational reflection (*ākāraparivitakka*), and cogitation upon a view (*diṭṭhinijjhānakkhanti*)—all of which have a twofold result in this life, being capable of turning out either true or false [Kalupahana 1976; Jayatilleke 1963; Evans]. In response, the Buddha delineates a graduated path distinguishing the mere preservation or safeguarding of truth (*saccānurakkhaṇa*), awakening to truth (*saccānubodha*), and the ultimate attainment of truth (*saccānuppatti*) through personal transformation and meditative cultivation under a virtuous teacher [SuttaCentral; Evans].
Close parallels to specific pericopes appear in the Mūlasarvāstivāda *Vinayavastu* (*Saṅghabhedavastu*) and related texts [Peipina 2008; DharmaNexus]. Within the Pali canon, the sutta shares extensive formulas with other dialogues involving brahmins, especially the *Soṇadaṇḍa Sutta* (DN 4), *Kūṭadanta Sutta* (DN 5), *Ambaṭṭha Sutta* (DN 3), and *Tevijja Sutta* (DN 13), notably the standard list of ten ancient brahmin seers [Black 2011; SuttaCentral; DharmaNexus].
